In montane populations of the Long-legged wood frog (Rana macrocnemis) inhabiting the Caucasus region, breeding typically commences soon after snowmelt in shallow, ephemeral water bodies. Reproductive output, based on field observations of gravid females, appears comparatively modest for a ranid of its size. Each female typically deposits a single clutch containing 233 eggs [N_R_i = Each female typically deposits a single clutch containing 233 eggs], with the species generally producing one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year] under natural conditions at an average water temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. Hatchlings emerge after a relatively short embryonic period; laboratory incubation at 10 °C [T = 10 °C] indicates that the age at hatching is 20 days [ab = 20 days]. The tiny neonates are barely visible to the naked eye, weighing a mere 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams] at birth. This extremely low initial mass reflects the species' highly fecund, small-egg life-history strategy, which is crucial for exploiting transient breeding habitats where rapid larval development is essential before seasonal desiccation.

Sexual maturation in Rana macrocnemis occurs at a remarkably consistent body size across both sexes, a trait shared with several other Palearctic brown frogs. Snout-vent length data from preserved specimens indicate that both females and males reach puberty at 4 centimeters [Lp = 4 centimeters]. This uniform size at maturity suggests a shared physiological threshold governing the onset of reproductive capability, likely linked to reaching a minimum body mass that can support the energetic demands of gonad development. The age at which this size threshold is reached, observed in tadpoles reared under controlled conditions at 10 °C [T = 10 °C], is 4 years since birth [tp = 4 years since birth]. This relatively prolonged juvenile phase, spanning four years from hatching, highlights a slow pace of life for a temperate-zone amphibian. During this extended larval and post-metamorphic period, individuals accumulate substantial energy reserves, which are subsequently channeled into the first breeding effort. The transition from the aquatic larval stage to the terrestrial juvenile form is itself a critical milestone in this developmental timeline.

As tadpoles develop in cool montane streams and ponds, the transition to a terrestrial existence is a protracted process calibrated to the local thermal regime. Laboratory studies conducted at a constant 10 °C [T = 10 °C] have shown that the time from egg hatching to the completion of metamorphosis is 2.5 years . This remarkably long larval duration, spanning two and a half years, stands in contrast to many lowland ranids that complete metamorphosis in a single season. Such an extended larval phase is likely an adaptation to low productivity and cold temperatures in high-altitude habitats, allowing tadpoles to grow slowly but steadily until they reach a sufficient size for tail resorption and limb development. Following metamorphosis, the juvenile froglets, known as metamorphlings, emerge onto land with a full set of terrestrial adaptations. At this point, their body mass has increased substantially from the minuscule hatchling weight, setting the stage for the next phase of somatic growth that will ultimately lead to reproductive maturity.

Adult body size in Rana macrocnemis exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism, with females attaining a larger ultimate snout-vent length than males. The maximum recorded snout-vent length for adult females is 5.9 centimeters [Li = 5.9 centimeters], whereas adult males reach a slightly smaller asymptotic size of 5.5 centimeters [Li = 5.5 centimeters]. This size disparity is typical of many ranid frogs and is often attributed to fecundity selection favouring larger females capable of producing more eggs. Accompanying this difference in length, the ultimate wet weights also show a clear divergence: the heaviest females weighed in at 40 grams [Wwi = 40 grams], while the largest males recorded a mature body mass of 32.4 grams [Wwi = 32.4 grams]. At the onset of sexual maturity, when females first become capable of reproduction, their wet weight averages approximately 7 grams [Wwp = approximately 7 grams], indicating substantial post-pubertal growth is required to reach the full adult size before peak reproductive output is achieved.

Longevity is another key life-history parameter that shapes the population dynamics of this high-elevation amphibian, with individuals displaying a notably slow pace of aging. The maximum lifespan recorded for Rana macrocnemis under semi-natural conditions at a thermal regime of 10 °C [T = 10 °C] is 11 years [am = 11 years]. This extended longevity, exceeding a decade, allows for multiple breeding seasons over an individual's lifetime, thereby compensating for the low annual fecundity of a single clutch. The combination of a late age at first reproduction, a single clutch per year, and a long adult lifespan places this species firmly on the slow end of the amphibian life-history continuum. The trade-off between early reproduction and survival is clearly resolved in favour of persistence, a strategy well-suited to the unpredictable and harsh environment of the Caucasus Mountains, where suitable breeding opportunities may be infrequent. These demographic traits collectively ensure population stability despite occasional years of reproductive failure.
